core_concepts: Ongoing substernal pain at rest with arm radiation and major cardiovascular risk factors must be treated as possible acute coronary syndrome until urgent assessment excludes it.
ACS includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI; symptoms alone do not reliably distinguish them.
Initial evaluation requires urgent ECG-based assessment and cardiac troponin testing within an emergency pathway; treatment then depends on ACS subtype, bleeding risk, and reperfusion strategy.
diagnostic_clues: Two hours of pain at rest
Substernal pain radiating to the left arm
Hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and family history of myocardial infarction
common_misconceptions: Antacid response or non-response is not enough to confirm or exclude ACS.
A patient describing pain as heartburn does not make a gastrointestinal diagnosis safe.
Absence of every classic symptom does not rule out ACS.
dangerous_errors: Reassuring or discharging the patient as reflux before urgent ACS evaluation
Delaying emergency escalation while completing a routine outpatient history
Claiming that a single symptom, ECG, or troponin result always rules ACS in or out
management_principles: Escalate promptly to an acute chest-pain/ACS pathway and monitor the patient.
Use ECG, serial troponin assessment, and the full clinical context rather than one symptom in isolation.
Use antithrombotic and reperfusion strategies according to the working diagnosis, contraindications, bleeding risk, and local emergency protocol.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Exact drug selection, dose, and invasive timing depend on ECG findings, troponin results, contraindications, bleeding risk, and local protocol.
Other immediately dangerous causes of chest pain, including aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism, remain in the differential when supported by the presentation.

source_refs.title: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for Acute Coronary Syndromes

doorknob_disclosure: you have actually had a few of these same chest pains over the past two weeks, but they went away, so you told yourself it was nothing and didn't want to make a fuss about it

reference_soap.subjective: 58M presenting with 2hr substernal chest pain 7/10, radiating to left arm, onset at rest. Denies relief with antacids. PMH: HTN, T2DM. Smokes 20 pack-years.
reference_soap.assessment: ACS until proven otherwise. DDx: STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina, aortic dissection, PE.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent acute chest-pain/ACS pathway with monitoring, ECG and serial troponin assessment; give aspirin when appropriate and not contraindicated, provide oxygen only if clinically indicated for hypoxemia, establish IV access, and obtain urgent cardiology/emergency input. Further antithrombotic and reperfusion management depends on findings, contraindications, bleeding risk, and local protocol.

learning_objectives: Elicit cardiac history systematically using SOCRATES
Explore cardiac risk factors: HTN, DM, smoking, family Hx, dyslipidaemia
Address patient's ICE — especially fear of MI
Verbalize ACS differential and dangerous diagnosis first

teaching.one_liner: Chest pain from a blocked or critically narrowed coronary artery — the one diagnosis you must exclude first in any adult with chest pain.
red_flags: Pain lasting over 20 minutes at rest, sweating, low blood pressure, or fainting

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
When did it start, and how long does it last each time?
How would you describe it — sharp, crushing, burning, tight?
Along with the pain, did you feel sweaty, sick, or short of breath?
Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and do you smoke?

must_ask.objective: Family history of early heart disease
must_ask.say: Has anyone in your family had a heart attack, especially young?
What are you most worried this might be?
